Y’all be mad about the WRONG scammers! Not me! Healthcare might be the biggest scam there is!

UnitedHealth Group reportedly made $6.2 BILLION in profit in one quarter while denying about 32% of prior authorization requests. You pay your premiums, deductibles and copays, then when your DOCTOR says you need something, the insurance company can still say NO. Meanwhile they keep your money. 

So, pay your premium, get seen by a doctor, claim gets denied. They keep your money. Thats crazy math!… $6.2 BILLION.

But we’ll raise hell about somebody getting a couple hundred dollars in assistance. Y’all mad at the wrong people. FOLLOW THE MONEY! 🎯
UnitedHealth denial rate is 33%. For in network claims.
“United Healthcare posted $6.2 billion in profits while simultaneously denying 32% of all claims.”

Denying your claim isn't a mistake. It's the business model.

Follow the incentive and it lines up.

UnitedHealth Group cleared $6.1 billion in profit last quarter.

In that same stretch, it denied 31% of prior authorization requests.

One out of every three medical requests said no.

That's not a glitch.

It's the system doing exactly what it was built to do.

Every dollar not paid to a patient stays on the balance sheet.

Approve less. Keep more.

You paid your premium every month, on time, no questions asked.

Then you got sick, or hurt, or scared.

And the answer came back no.

The money didn't vanish. It just didn't go to you.

None of this needs a conspiracy.

It just needs a company running the math on what denial does to profit.

Insurers say prior authorization stops unnecessary care.

Sometimes that's even true.

But a one-in-three denial rate isn't quality control.

It's a numbers game, and you're the number.

That's the part that should make everyone uncomfortable.

items.postText: United Healthcare had quarterly profits of $6.2 billion while denying 32% of all claims. You paid your premium, they denied your coverage but kept your premiums.

Straight, No Chaser Health: The Prior Auth Scam

Let’s stop pretending the math is complicated. It isn’t. The viral 32% prior‑authorization denial rate making the rounds isn’t a myth — it’s straight from Senate and congressional investigations. Those reports show that UnitedHealthcare’s Medicare Advantage plans have denial baked directly into the business model.

And while patients, clinicians, and families jump through endless hoops, UnitedHealth Group just posted roughly $6.2 billion in quarterly profit. That’s not an accident. That’s intent. That’s not a rounding error. That’s the business model.

Here’s the view from inside: if you work in post‑acute care, rehab, or complex medical management, you already know the truth. Denial rates spike even higher exactly when patients are most vulnerable — when clinicians are trying to prevent deterioration, readmission, or long‑term disability. The moment care matters most is the moment the system seems most likely to say no.

So let’s call this what it is: prior authorization has become a mechanism for denying medically necessary care in service of profit extraction.

The question isn’t whether the system is broken.
The question is: broken for whom?

How is it that we have an 80% approval rating for our current system? Because from where patients and clinicians sit, the harm is obvious. But from where shareholders sit, the profits are historic.

And that tension — unchecked, unregulated, and increasingly normalized — is becoming one of the most dangerous fault lines in American healthcare.

Rooting for the home team isn’t always patriotism. When we can do better, we should be introspective enough to do so. If we’re not, we’re just the willingly duped in an advanced form of a scam.

#AskSterlingMD #straightnochaserhealth #KnowledgeIsHealth #HealthSelfEmpowerment

items.postText: Uhc just made $6.2B last quarter and denied 32% of health claims. One out of three claims denied. They kept your money you paid them. You paid twice for your procedure. And it’s legal.

$100 MILLION.

That's the reported amount Lee Health says is tied up in disputed claims with UnitedHealthcare.

Regardless of how the dispute is ultimately resolved, that number should get the attention of every healthcare CFO, practice administrator and physician owner.

Because this isn't just a Lee Health–UnitedHealthcare story.

It's a revenue integrity story.

And it raises a much bigger question for healthcare organizations:

If reimbursement and claims disputes can reach this magnitude at a major health system, what's happening at organizations that don't have the same resources, technology and staff to identify potential revenue leakage?

Your organization doesn't need a $100 million problem for it to matter.

It could be $1 million.

$250,000.

$50,000.

The more important question is:

Would you know?

Most organizations closely monitor denials and A/R.

But there's another question worth asking:

Who independently verifies that the insurance payments you receive match what your payer contracts say you should receive?

Because "paid" and "paid correctly" aren't necessarily the same thing.

#RevenueIntegrity #HealthcareFinance #healthcarecfo #RevenueCycle #RCM #underpayments #PayerContracts
